A10 terms
ABC PLEASE

A DBT framework for strengthening everyday emotional resilience.

ABC PLEASE combines positive experiences, growing competence, rehearsing difficult situations, and caring for physical health. It supports emotion regulation over time rather than serving only as a crisis response.

Category:

See also

  • Accumulate Positive Emotions
  • Build Mastery
  • Cope Ahead
  • PLEASE

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 14, p. 247

Learn more (1)

  • Accumulating Positive Emotions
Acceptance

Also called: expansion

Allowing present inner experience without making its removal a condition for action.

In ACT, acceptance means making room for thoughts, feelings, or sensations while choosing how to act. It does not mean approving harm, abandoning boundaries, or giving up on change.

Category:

See also

  • Psychological Flexibility
  • Willingness

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Chapters 4 and 9
  • The Happiness Trap (supplied 33-chapter edition): Russ Harris, Chapters 10-14

Learn more (1)

  • Making Room for Experience
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy

Also called: ACT

An approach that supports flexible, values-guided action alongside difficult inner experiences.

ACT develops ways to notice thoughts and feelings, make room for them when useful, and act in personally meaningful directions. Its aim is greater flexibility, rather than eliminating every uncomfortable thought or feeling.

Category:

See also

  • Acceptance
  • Cognitive Defusion
  • Psychological Flexibility
  • Values

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Introduction; Chapters 4-13

Learn more (1)

  • Making Room for Experience
ACCEPTS

Also called: Wise Mind ACCEPTS

A DBT set of distraction options for getting through a period of intense distress.

ACCEPTS offers different ways to shift attention temporarily, such as a task, helping someone, or another mental focus. The purpose is to reduce immediate risk and return to the issue when more able to respond.

Category:

See also

  • Crisis Survival
  • Self-Soothe
  • IMPROVE

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Distress Tolerance Handout 7, p. 333
Accumulate Positive Emotions

Also called: Accumulating Positive Emotions

Building opportunities for positive experience now and a more meaningful life over time.

Short-term practice includes accessible enjoyable activities and noticing them while they happen. Longer-term practice involves values, goals, and achievable steps. It does not require pretending that painful circumstances are positive.

Category:

See also

  • ABC PLEASE
  • Values
  • Behavioural Activation

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handouts 15 and 17, pp. 248, 252

Learn more (1)

  • Building Mastery & Cope Ahead
Action Urge

Also called: Action Urges

The impulse to act in a particular way that accompanies an emotion.

An urge may involve approaching, withdrawing, confronting, or another response. Feeling the urge does not require acting on it. Facts, safety, and your goals help determine what response is useful.

Category:

See also

  • Opposite Action
  • Functions of Emotions

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 3, p. 210; Handout 5, p. 213

Learn more (1)

  • Emotions
Activity Monitoring

Noticing connections between everyday activities, mood, and engagement.

Brief observations before and after an activity can reveal patterns involving enjoyment, connection, or accomplishment. They help guide adjustments rather than grading productivity or requiring immediate mood improvement.

Category:

See also

  • Behavioural Activation

References

  • Mind Over Mood, Second Edition (2016): Dennis Greenberger and Christine A. Padesky, Chapter 13

Learn more (1)

  • Maintaining Progress
Anger

An emotion often connected with perceived threat, unfairness, or an obstructed goal.

Anger can energise action and signal that something matters. The feeling does not by itself prove wrongdoing or require aggression; facts and effectiveness help guide how to respond.

Category:

See also

  • Action Urge
  • Check the Facts

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 6, p. 214

Learn more (1)

  • Anger
Attentional Flexibility

Shifting, broadening, or returning attention as the situation requires.

Rather than holding attention perfectly on one object, this skill allows you to notice distraction and reorient. The chosen focus can be external and adapted to your sensory needs.

Category:

See also

  • Present-Moment Awareness

References

  • The Happiness Trap (supplied 33-chapter edition): Russ Harris, Chapters 17-20

Learn more (1)

  • Returning to the Present
Automatic Thought

Also called: Automatic Thoughts

A thought or mental image that arises without deliberate effort.

Automatic thoughts are quick interpretations of a situation. Noticing one allows you to examine its accuracy and usefulness instead of treating it as an established fact.

Category:

See also

  • Cognitive Model
  • Core Belief

References

  • Beck Institute: Cognitive Model

Learn more (1)

  • Working with Anger, Guilt & Shame
B9 terms
Balanced Thought

Also called: balanced alternative

An interpretation that takes relevant evidence and uncertainty into account.

A balanced thought can acknowledge a real difficulty and possible ways to respond. It is not necessarily positive, and its usefulness does not depend on removing an emotion immediately.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Cognitive Behavioural Therapy

References

  • Mind Over Mood, Second Edition (2016): Dennis Greenberger and Christine A. Padesky, Chapters 8-10

Learn more (1)

  • Thought Records Part 2
Behaviour Chain Analysis

Also called: Behavior Chain, Behavior Chain Analysis, Chain Analysis

A close look at the sequence leading to a behaviour and what follows it.

A chain analysis connects the situation, thoughts, feelings, body responses, actions, and consequences surrounding a specific behaviour. It helps locate points for a different response and identify repair or prevention needs.

Category:

See also

  • Prompting Event
  • Vulnerability Factors
  • Consequences
  • Missing-Links Analysis

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, General Handouts 6-7a, pp. 19-22

Learn more (1)

  • Behaviour Chain Analysis and Missing Links
Behavioural Activation

Also called: Behavioral Activation

Planning manageable activities that support engagement with daily life.

Behavioural activation works with the cycle of low mood and reduced activity. Choose achievable actions connected to care, connection, enjoyment, or accomplishment, and notice what happens rather than waiting for motivation to arrive first.

Category:

See also

  • Values

References

  • Mind Over Mood, Second Edition: Dennis Greenberger and Christine A. Padesky, Chapter 13, pp. 188-218

Learn more (2)

  • Behaviour Activation
  • Maintaining Progress
Behavioural Experiment

Also called: Behavioral Experiment, Behavioral Experiments, Behavioural Experiments

A planned activity used to test a prediction.

A behavioural experiment compares what you expect with what actually happens. The result provides evidence to reconsider a belief.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Core Belief

References

  • Beck Institute: Cognitive Model

Learn more (1)

  • Assumptions & Core Beliefs
Being Mind

A mode of attention that is curious about experience without needing to achieve something.

Being mind makes space to notice the present as it is. It can complement planning and problem solving, rather than requiring you to give up responsibilities or goals.

Category:

See also

  • Doing Mind
  • Wise Mind

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 9, p. 71

Learn more (1)

  • Being Mind and Doing Mind
Biosocial Theory

A DBT account of how biology and social responses can interact to shape emotional difficulties.

Emotional sensitivity and difficulties regulating responses can develop through ongoing interaction with the environment. The model looks at these influences together, rather than treating distress as a character flaw or assigning one person all the blame.

Category:

See also

  • Emotional Vulnerability
  • Invalidation

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, General Handout 5, pp. 14-15
Body Scan

Also called: Body Scan Meditation

Moving attention through areas of the body to notice present sensations.

A body scan is an awareness practice, not a test of relaxation. Notice sensations or their absence with curiosity. You can adapt or pause the practice if attending inward becomes unhelpful.

Category:

See also

  • Observe
  • Mindfulness

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 1a, p. 46; Distress Tolerance Handout 8a, p. 335
Build Mastery

Also called: Building Mastery

Developing a sense of capability through manageable challenges and practice.

Choose tasks that stretch your abilities without setting you up for repeated failure. Adjust difficulty as you learn. Mastery grows through participation and progress, not only through flawless results.

Category:

See also

  • ABC PLEASE
  • Shaping
  • Cope Ahead

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 19, p. 256

Learn more (1)

  • Building Mastery & Cope Ahead
Burning Bridges and Building New Ones

Reducing routes back to an addictive behaviour while creating alternative responses to cravings.

The DBT skill combines changing access and cues with competing mental images, sensory experiences, or other responses. It is a recovery-planning concept, not a general instruction to cut off relationships.

Category:

See also

  • Clear Mind
  • Urge Surfing

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Distress Tolerance Handout 20, p. 362
C12 terms
Check the Facts

Examining whether an emotional interpretation fits the available evidence.

Separate observations from assumptions, consider other explanations, and examine the threat you anticipate. This skill also asks whether the emotion's intensity fits the situation; it does not mean dismissing the feeling.

Category:

See also

  • Describe
  • Opposite Action
  • Problem Solving

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 8, p. 228

Learn more (2)

  • Check the Facts
  • Examples of Emotions That Fit the Facts
Clear Mind

A recovery stance that recognises progress while staying aware of vulnerability to relapse.

Clear mind combines engagement in recovery with realistic attention to cues and urges. It avoids both being driven by the addictive behaviour and assuming that current success removes all future risk.

Category:

See also

  • Dialectical Abstinence
  • Urge Surfing

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Distress Tolerance Handout 18, p. 359
Cognitive Behavioural Therapy

Also called: CBT, Cognitive Behavior Therapy, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, Cognitive Behaviour Therapy

A therapy that works with patterns in thinking and behaviour.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy combines cognitive and behavioural approaches. It helps people examine interpretations and try different actions, rather than assuming that a distressing thought must be true.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Cognitive Model

References

  • APA Dictionary of Psychology: cognitive behavior therapy

Learn more (1)

  • Introduction to CBT
Cognitive Defusion

Also called: Defusion, unhooking

Noticing a thought as a thought rather than automatically obeying it.

Defusion changes your relationship to thinking. You can notice a prediction or self-judgment and choose your response without having to prove the thought false or force it to stop.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Self-as-Context

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Chapter 6, pp. 69-86
  • The Happiness Trap (supplied 33-chapter edition): Russ Harris, Chapters 4-6

Learn more (1)

  • Thoughts & the Observing Perspective
Cognitive Fusion

Treating a thought as an instruction or unquestioned account of reality.

Fusion describes moments when thoughts strongly organise behaviour and other available information receives less attention. Defusion creates room to consider a thought without automatically following it.

Category:

See also

  • Cognitive Defusion

References

  • The Happiness Trap (supplied 33-chapter edition): Russ Harris, Chapters 4-6

Learn more (1)

  • Thoughts & the Observing Perspective
Cognitive Model

An account of how interpretations influence feelings, body responses, and actions.

The cognitive model connects a situation with its personal meaning and the responses that follow. Beliefs shape those interpretations; examining them can reveal other ways of understanding the situation.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Core Belief

References

  • Beck Institute: Cognitive Model
Committed Action

Taking and reviewing practical steps guided by your values.

Committed action turns a valued direction into behaviour. It includes adjusting plans after obstacles and beginning again, rather than demanding perfect persistence with a plan that no longer fits.

Category:

See also

  • Values
  • Willingness

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Chapter 13, pp. 177-194
  • The Happiness Trap (supplied 33-chapter edition): Russ Harris, Chapters 27-32

Learn more (1)

  • Values & Committed Action
Community Reinforcement

Making recovery more rewarding through supportive people, activities, and surroundings.

The DBT skill focuses on building sources of connection and satisfaction that support life without the addictive behaviour. It recognises that the environment matters, rather than relying on determination alone.

Category:

See also

  • Reinforcement
  • Dialectical Abstinence

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Distress Tolerance Handout 19, p. 361
Consequences

The immediate and later effects of a behaviour.

A consequence can affect you, other people, or the situation. Short-term relief may help explain why an action repeats even when its later effects are costly. Consequences are not limited to punishment.

Category:

See also

  • Behaviour Chain Analysis
  • Reinforcement

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, General Handout 7a, p. 22
Cope Ahead

Also called: Coping Ahead

Rehearsing how you will use skills in a foreseeable difficult situation.

Identify the likely challenge and practise imagining yourself responding with a specific plan, including obstacles. Cope ahead develops readiness; it is more than repeatedly imagining everything that could go wrong.

Category:

See also

  • ABC PLEASE
  • Problem Solving

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 19, p. 256

Learn more (1)

  • Building Mastery & Cope Ahead
Core Belief

Also called: Core Beliefs

A broad belief about yourself, other people, or the world.

Core beliefs influence how you interpret experiences. In CBT, identifying and examining an unhelpful belief can support more balanced conclusions.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Cognitive Model

References

  • Beck Institute: Cognitive Model

Learn more (2)

  • Assumptions & Core Beliefs
  • Working with Anger, Guilt & Shame
Crisis Survival

Also called: Crisis Survival Skills

Short-term skills for intense distress when impulsive action could worsen the situation.

The immediate aim is to get through a difficult period with less harm and more ability to choose. Crisis survival skills are not intended to replace ongoing problem solving or emergency help when needed.

Category:

See also

  • Distress Tolerance
  • STOP
  • TIPP

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Distress Tolerance Handout 3, p. 326

Learn more (1)

  • Introduction & STOP
D9 terms
DEAR MAN

Also called: DEARMAN

A DBT framework for making a clear request or saying no while staying focused.

DEAR MAN combines describing the situation, expressing your position, asking clearly, and explaining useful consequences with focused, confident, flexible communication. It supports objectives effectiveness without guaranteeing that another person will agree.

Category:

See also

  • Objectives Effectiveness
  • GIVE
  • FAST

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Interpersonal Effectiveness Handout 5, pp. 125-126

Learn more (2)

  • DEAR + MAN
  • How to Ask & Say No & Troubleshooting
Describe

Also called: Describing

Putting observable experience into words while separating facts from interpretations.

Describe what you notice, including an inner experience as a thought or feeling. Saying that you notice a fear of rejection is different from claiming to know that someone will reject you.

Category:

See also

  • WHAT Skills
  • Observe
  • Check the Facts

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 4, p. 53

Learn more (2)

  • Describe
  • Observe
Dialectical Abstinence

Combining a commitment to stop an addictive behaviour with a plan to limit harm and recover after a lapse.

The approach holds a clear change goal alongside realistic preparation for difficulty. A lapse calls for renewed support and a return to the plan, rather than an all-or-nothing conclusion that further effort is pointless.

Category:

See also

  • Clear Mind
  • Cope Ahead

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Distress Tolerance Handout 17, p. 357
Dialectical Behaviour Therapy

Also called: DBT, Dialectical Behavior Therapy, Dialectical Behavioral Therapy, Dialectical Behavioural Therapy

A therapy that combines behavioural change methods with mindfulness and acceptance.

Dialectical Behaviour Therapy brings together behavioural approaches and mindfulness. DBT skills training teaches practical ways to manage distress, emotions, attention, and relationships; a skills website is only one educational resource, not a complete DBT treatment programme.

Categories: , , ,

See also

  • Mindfulness
  • Wise Mind

References

  • APA Dictionary of Psychology: dialectical behavior therapy
  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, General Handouts 1 and 5, pp. 9, 14-15
Dialectics

Also called: Dialectical Thinking

Looking for multiple connected truths while recognising change and mutual influence.

A dialectical approach questions rigid either-or conclusions. Acceptance of a present difficulty can coexist with efforts to change it. The aim is to develop a more complete understanding, not to declare every position equally accurate.

Category:

See also

  • Walking the Middle Path
  • Dialectical Behaviour Therapy

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Interpersonal Effectiveness Handouts 15-16, pp. 150-151
DIME Game

Also called: The DIME Game

A structured way to consider how firmly to ask for something or decline it.

The DIME Game weighs context such as rights, capacity, priorities, timing, and the relationship. It supports judgment about intensity rather than creating an obligation to ask, agree, or refuse.

Category:

See also

  • Interpersonal Priorities
  • DEAR MAN

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Interpersonal Effectiveness Handout 8, pp. 131-133; Worksheet 6, pp. 176-177
Disgust

An emotion that can involve revulsion and an urge to distance yourself from something.

Disgust may arise around perceived contamination, violation, or other aversive experiences. Learned interpretations also influence it, so feeling disgust does not establish that a person or situation is harmful.

Category:

See also

  • Action Urge
  • Check the Facts

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 6, p. 215

Learn more (1)

  • Disgust
Distress Tolerance

Skills for getting through painful experiences and responding to realities that cannot immediately be changed.

Distress tolerance includes short-term crisis skills and practices of acceptance. It can create room for a safer next choice, while problem solving and longer-term changes may still be needed.

Category:

See also

  • Crisis Survival
  • Radical Acceptance
  • Emotion Regulation

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Distress Tolerance Handout 1, p. 321
Doing Mind

A mode of attention organised around tasks, solutions, and goals.

Doing mind helps you plan and act. When it dominates, every experience can become a problem to fix. DBT explores balancing purposeful action with openness to the present.

Category:

See also

  • Being Mind
  • Wise Mind

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 9, p. 71

Learn more (1)

  • Being Mind and Doing Mind
E9 terms
Effectively

Also called: Effectiveness

Choosing actions that work toward your goals in the situation that actually exists.

Effectiveness asks what is likely to help, taking circumstances and consequences into account. It can mean loosening the need to win an argument while still protecting your values and boundaries.

Category:

See also

  • HOW Skills
  • Wise Mind
  • Self-Respect Effectiveness

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 5, p. 60

Learn more (2)

  • Effectively
  • Non-Judgmentally
Emotion Mind

A state in which feelings and urges strongly guide your response.

Emotion Mind gives priority to emotional information. Other facts or longer-term goals can become harder to consider.

Category:

See also

  • Reasonable Mind
  • Wise Mind

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 3, p. 50
Emotion Model

Also called: Describing Emotions, Model for Describing Emotions

A way to map how an emotional response develops and affects what happens next.

The model connects vulnerabilities, an event, interpretations, bodily changes, awareness, urges, expressions, and aftereffects. These parts influence one another, so there may be several places to intervene.

Category:

See also

  • Prompting Event
  • Action Urge
  • Secondary Emotion

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 5, p. 213

Emotion Regulation

Also called: Emotional Regulation

Skills for understanding emotions and influencing how you respond to them.

Emotion regulation includes identifying feelings, reducing vulnerability, and choosing useful responses. The goal is not to eliminate emotions; feelings can provide information even when their intensity or urges need attention.

Category:

See also

  • Check the Facts
  • Opposite Action
  • ABC PLEASE

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 1, p. 205

Learn more (1)

  • What Emotions Do for You
Emotional Vulnerability

A tendency or current condition that makes strong emotional reactions more likely.

Some people react quickly or intensely and take longer to settle. Stress, illness, sleep disruption, and other circumstances can also increase vulnerability. Understanding these factors helps guide support and skills practice.

Category:

See also

  • Biosocial Theory
  • Vulnerability Factors
  • PLEASE

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 4, p. 211; General Handout 5, pp. 14-15
Envy

An emotion arising when someone else has something important that you want and lack.

Envy can draw attention to an unmet wish, opportunity, or need. It differs from jealousy about losing something already valued, and it need not determine how you treat the other person.

Category:

See also

  • Jealousy
  • Values

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 6, p. 216

Learn more (1)

  • Envy
Evidence Gathering

Collecting concrete observations to evaluate or refine an interpretation.

Useful evidence separates what happened from what you inferred. Include information that fits and information that complicates a belief; a single ambiguous observation may not settle the question.

Category:

See also

  • Behavioural Experiment
  • Balanced Thought

References

  • Mind Over Mood, Second Edition (2016): Dennis Greenberger and Christine A. Padesky, Chapters 8 and 10-12

Learn more (1)

  • Assumptions & Core Beliefs
Experiential Avoidance

Attempts to escape inner experiences that can become costly or restrictive.

Avoiding a thought, feeling, memory, or sensation is not always a problem. In ACT, the concern is a rigid pattern that narrows life or prevents useful action even when the strategy has lasting costs.

Category:

See also

  • Acceptance
  • Psychological Flexibility

References

  • The Happiness Trap (supplied 33-chapter edition): Russ Harris, Chapters 2-3

Learn more (1)

  • Making Room for Experience
Extinction

The weakening of a learned behaviour when its maintaining reinforcement stops.

A response may initially increase or vary before it decreases. Extinction does not teach a replacement skill, and behaviour can return. The concept does not justify ignoring distress or withholding essential care.

Category:

See also

  • Reinforcement
  • Shaping

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Interpersonal Effectiveness Handout 21, p. 162
F3 terms
FAST

A DBT reminder for protecting self-respect during an interaction.

FAST emphasises fairness, avoiding unnecessary apologies, staying connected to values, and honesty. Avoiding over-apology does not mean refusing to acknowledge harm or make a warranted apology.

Category:

See also

  • Self-Respect Effectiveness
  • Values
  • DEAR MAN

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Interpersonal Effectiveness Handout 7, p. 130

Learn more (1)

  • DEAR + FAST
Fear

An emotion organised around perceived danger or threat.

Fear can prepare protection, escape, or caution. Assess the situation before deciding what to do; an alarm can be important without every feared outcome being certain.

Category:

See also

  • Check the Facts
  • Action Urge

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 6, p. 217

Learn more (1)

  • Fear
Functions of Emotions

Also called: What Emotions Do

The ways emotions prepare action and communicate information to ourselves and others.

Emotions can highlight needs or threats and influence how other people respond. They are useful signals to examine, but their presence or strength does not by itself establish the facts of a situation.

Category:

See also

  • Action Urge
  • Check the Facts

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 3, p. 210

Learn more (1)

  • What Emotions Do for You
G2 terms
GIVE

A DBT reminder to approach an interaction with care for the relationship.

GIVE brings together gentleness, interest, validation, and an approachable manner. These qualities can support a difficult conversation while leaving room for boundaries and disagreement.

Category:

See also

  • Relationship Effectiveness
  • Validation
  • DEAR MAN

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Interpersonal Effectiveness Handout 6, p. 128

Learn more (1)

  • DEAR + GIVE
Guilt

An emotion connected with believing you have violated a value or caused harm.

Guilt can motivate repair when it fits the facts. Feeling responsible does not always mean you are responsible; consider what happened, what was within your control, and what proportionate action could help.

Category:

See also

  • Shame
  • Check the Facts
  • Values

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 6, p. 223

Learn more (1)

  • Guilt
H4 terms
Half-Smiling

Also called: Half Smile

Using a relaxed face and a slight smile as a practice of bodily openness.

The expression is gentle rather than a forced performance of happiness. Half-smiling is explored as support for acceptance, not as proof that you are happy with what happened.

Category:

See also

  • Willing Hands
  • Radical Acceptance

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Distress Tolerance Handout 14, p. 347
Happiness

A family of positive emotional experiences, including enjoyment, contentment, and joy.

Happiness may accompany connection, achievement, relief, or a pleasant experience. Its intensity varies; quieter satisfaction counts too. Noticing a positive moment does not erase other feelings or difficulties.

Category:

See also

  • Accumulate Positive Emotions
  • Mindfulness of Current Emotions

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Emotion Regulation Handout 6, p. 218

Learn more (1)

  • Happiness
Hot Thought

A thought or meaning closely connected to a strong emotional response in a situation.

Identifying a hot thought helps focus a thought record on the interpretation that matters emotionally. The most upsetting thought is not automatically the most accurate one.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Balanced Thought

References

  • Mind Over Mood, Second Edition (2016): Dennis Greenberger and Christine A. Padesky, Chapters 6-7

Learn more (1)

  • Thought Records Part 2
HOW Skills

The qualities Non-Judgmentally, One-Mindfully, and Effectively.

HOW Skills describe how to practise a WHAT skill. These qualities can be used together.

Category:

See also

  • Mindfulness
  • WHAT Skills

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015): Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 5, p. 60

Learn more (3)

  • Effectively
  • Non-Judgmentally
  • One-Mindfully
I5 terms
IMPROVE

Also called: IMPROVE the Moment

A DBT collection of ways to make a difficult moment more bearable.

IMPROVE draws on imagination, meaning, spiritual support if relevant, relaxation, present focus, a brief break, and encouragement. Choose what fits; using the skill does not require liking or denying the situation.

Interpersonal Effectiveness

Skills for pursuing interpersonal goals while considering relationships and self-respect.

Love

Noticing an emotion as a changing experience without automatically following its urge.

This analysis looks for barriers such as unclear expectations, not remembering, low willingness, or practical obstacles. The purpose is to choose a workable support for next time, rather than to conclude that someone did not care.

Negative Reinforcement

An increase in behaviour because it removes or reduces something unpleasant.

Relief can make an action more likely to repeat. For example, avoiding a task may be reinforced when anxiety briefly falls. Negative reinforcement increases behaviour; it is not another name for punishment.

Nonjudgmentally

Also called: Nonjudgmentalness

Objectives Effectiveness

Opposite Action

Choosing behaviour opposite to an emotional urge when the urge does not fit the facts or acting on it is ineffective.

After considering the situation and safety, change the response that would otherwise maintain the emotion. Opposite action is not a rule to ignore accurate danger signals or suppress every uncomfortable feeling.

An increase in behaviour because something rewarding follows it.

The word positive means that something is added, not that the behaviour is morally good. Recognition after practising a skill may be reinforcing if it makes future practice more likely.

Psychological flexibility combines awareness and openness with useful action. It includes changing course when needed instead of letting rigid rules or attempts to avoid every uncomfortable feeling determine your choices.

An emotion often associated with loss, separation, disappointment, or unmet hopes.

Wise Mind

Wise Mind is the integrated perspective that draws on both emotion and reason.

Wise Mind is a DBT concept for the integrated perspective that draws on both emotional experience and reasonable thinking. It supports noticing what is true, what matters, and what an effective next step may be.

Workability

How well a response serves a chosen direction in its actual context.

A workability check considers immediate effects and longer-term consequences. It asks whether a strategy helps you participate in what matters, rather than judging it only by whether it reduces discomfort.
